💍 Introduction: spreading data across servers

Hinglish samajh: Jab ek server kaafi nahi hota to hum kai servers lagate hain, aur sawaal uthta hai ki kaunsi request ya data kis server par jaye. Hum chahte hain ki load barabar baante aur server jodte ya hatate samay kam se kam data hile. Consistent hashing ye dono deta hai, aur DynamoDB, Cassandra, Discord, Akamai CDN aur Maglev load balancer isse use karte hain. Pehle hum simple modulo hashing ki samasya dekhenge, phir hash ring, virtual nodes aur ek real experiment.

When one server cannot handle all the traffic or hold all the data, we use many servers. This is horizontal scaling. But then a new question appears: for each request or piece of data, which server should handle it? We want two things. First, the work should be spread evenly, so no server becomes a hotspot while others sit idle. Second, when we add or remove a server, as little data as possible should have to move.

Consistent hashing is the technique that gives us both. It is used inside many famous systems: Amazon DynamoDB, Apache Cassandra, Discord, the Akamai CDN and the Maglev load balancer all use it. Any time you see a system that can add servers without a big reshuffle, consistent hashing is probably behind it.

We will first look at the simple approach (the hash modulo N) and see why it breaks. Then we will meet the hash ring, learn how lookups, additions and removals work, fix the uneven spread with virtual nodes, and finally try it with real numbers.

✨ Features

  • Spreads data and requests across a pool of servers.
  • Remaps only a small fraction of keys when the pool changes.
  • Used by DynamoDB, Cassandra, Discord, Akamai and Maglev.

✅ Benefits

  • Horizontal scaling without large data moves.
  • Balanced load, fewer hotspots.
  • Servers can come and go safely.

⚠️ Problems

  • More complex than simple modulo hashing.
  • Needs virtual nodes to balance well.
  • Requires a good hash function.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Introduction

This chapter explores consistent hashing, a technique essential for achieving horizontal scaling by efficiently distributing requests and data across servers. It minimizes data redistribution when servers are added or removed and ensures an even distribution of data to mitigate issues like server hotspots.

Interview questions and answers

What problem does consistent hashing solve?
It distributes keys over servers evenly and, when servers are added or removed, it moves only a small fraction of the keys instead of almost all of them.
Where is it used in real systems?
Amazon DynamoDB, Apache Cassandra, Discord, the Akamai CDN and the Maglev load balancer.
Cross question: Why not just use a lookup table that maps keys to servers?
Such a table would be huge, must be shared and updated everywhere, and becomes a bottleneck. A hash computes the location without a table.
Which two properties do we want from a distribution scheme?
Even spread of load and minimal data movement when the server set changes.

💥 The rehashing problem with hash modulo N

Hinglish samajh: Sabse seedha tarika hai serverIndex = hash(key) % N, jahan N servers ki sankhya hai. Jab tak N badalta nahi, ye bilkul sahi chalta hai. Par jab server jodte ya hatate hain to N badal jaata hai aur lagbhag saari keys doosre server par chali jaati hain. Hamare example mein 8 mein se 6 keys hil gayin. Cache mein iska matlab hai bahut saare cache miss aur database par achanak bhaari load. Is rehashing problem ko consistent hashing se solve kiya jaata hai.

The simplest way to choose a server for a key is: serverIndex = hash(key) % N, where N is the number of servers. For example, with 4 servers numbered 0 to 3, a key whose hash is 18358617 goes to server 18358617 % 4 = 1. As long as the number of servers never changes, this works very well: keys are spread evenly and every client agrees where each key lives.

The trouble starts when N changes, which is exactly what happens when you scale or when a server fails. Now every key is divided by a new number, so most keys land on a different server. Look at this small example. With 4 servers, the eight keys go to servers 1, 0, 2, 0, 1, 3, 2, 3. If server 1 goes offline, N becomes 3 and the same keys go to 0, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 1, 0. Only 2 of the 8 keys stayed where they were. That is not just the keys of the dead server that moved, but nearly everything.

For a cache, this is a disaster. A client looks for a key on the new server, does not find it, and gets a cache miss. Suddenly a large share of the requests go to the database, which can overload it. The same happens when you add a server. A simulation I ran with 10,000 keys showed that going from 4 to 5 servers with hash % N moved about 79% of all keys. This is the rehashing problem, and consistent hashing was invented to fix it.

Eight keys with 4 servers, then 3 servers (server 1 offline)

✨ Features

  • Simple formula: hash(key) % N.
  • Perfect while N never changes.
  • Remaps most keys when N changes.

✅ Benefits

  • Very easy to implement and understand.
  • Even distribution when the pool is fixed.
  • No extra state needed.

⚠️ Problems

  • Removing a server reassigns most keys, causing cache misses.
  • Adding a server redistributes keys unnecessarily.
  • A sudden flood of misses can overload the database.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · The Rehashing Problem

Explanation

In traditional hashing methods, such as serverIndex = hash(key) % N, data redistribution becomes problematic when the number of servers changes. For example:

  • Removing a server causes most keys to be reassigned, leading to cache misses.
  • Adding a server results in unnecessary key redistributions.
  • This approach works well when the size of the server pool is fixed. However, problems arise when new servers are added, or existing servers are removed.

Key Issue

Redistribution of most keys when server count changes causes inefficiency and overload.

Interview questions and answers

What is the rehashing problem?
With serverIndex = hash(key) % N, changing N makes most keys map to different servers, so a large share of cached data is suddenly in the wrong place.
Why is it dangerous for caches?
The wrong server returns a cache miss, so requests go to the database, and the extra load can overload it.
Cross question: When is plain modulo hashing fine?
When the number of servers is fixed and you never need to add or remove nodes, or when moving the data is cheap.
How many keys move when going from 4 to 5 servers with modulo?
About 80% in theory (only keys whose hash gives the same remainder stay), and a simulation with 10,000 keys gave about 79%.

⭕ The hash ring: lookup, adding and removing servers

Hinglish samajh: Consistent hashing mein hash space ko ek ring (gola) ki tarah dekhte hain, jo 0 se 2^160-1 tak hai (SHA-1 ke saath). Pehle servers ko unke naam ya IP ka hash karke ring par rakhte hain, phir keys ko bhi usi hash function se ring par rakhte hain. Key ka server wo hai jo ghadi ki disha mein chalne par pehle milta hai. Naya server jodne par sirf uske aur pichhle server ke beech ki keys hilti hain, aur server hatane par sirf usi ki keys agle server par jaati hain. Baaki keys apni jagah rehti hain.

Consistent hashing is defined by one big idea: only a fraction of keys are remapped when servers are added or removed. To achieve this, we use a hash ring. Take a hash function such as SHA-1, whose output ranges from 0 to 2^160 - 1. Imagine these numbers written along a line from 0 (the start) to 2^160 - 1 (the end), and then bend the line so the two ends touch. You now have a ring, called the hash space.

First place the servers on the ring. Hash each server's name or IP address with the same hash function and put it at that position. Then place the keys on the ring by hashing them too. Notice that this hash has no modulo, so the number of servers does not affect where a key lands.

To find the server for a key, start at the key's position and move clockwise until you reach a server. That server owns the key. This is called server lookup. Every client that knows the ring layout gets the same answer.

Now the magic. When you add a server, it takes a spot on the ring. Only the keys between the new server and the previous server (going anticlockwise) now belong to the new server. All other keys stay exactly where they were. When you remove a server, only its keys are reassigned, to the next server clockwise. In both cases, only a small fraction of keys move, instead of almost all of them.

How it works, step by step

  1. Hash each server (by name or IP) onto the ring.
  2. Hash the key with the same function to place it on the ring.
  3. Walk clockwise from the key until you meet a server. That is the owner.
  4. To add a server, place it on the ring. It takes over only the keys between it and the previous server.
  5. To remove a server, delete it from the ring. Its keys move to the next server clockwise.

What changes when the server set changes

ChangeKeys affectedWhere they go
Add a serverKeys between the new server and its anticlockwise neighbourTo the new server
Remove a serverOnly the removed server's keysTo the next server clockwise
No change to the poolNoneStay the same

✨ Features

  • Hash space is a ring from 0 to 2^160 - 1 (with SHA-1).
  • Servers and keys use the same hash function.
  • Lookup walks clockwise to the first server.

✅ Benefits

  • Only a fraction of keys move when servers change.
  • Servers can be added or removed without reshuffling everything.
  • Every client computes the same placement.

⚠️ Problems

  • Servers may end up with very different amounts of the ring (uneven partitions).
  • Keys may be unevenly distributed.
  • Lookup needs an ordered structure (for example a sorted list) for speed.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Consistent Hashing

Definition

Consistent hashing ensures that only a fraction of keys are remapped when servers are added or removed. This minimizes disruptions and enhances scalability.

Key Concepts

  1. Hash Space and Ring: The hash space forms a continuous ring, with hash values distributed from 0 to 2^160-1 (e.g., using hash function like SHA-1). By connecting both ends we get a ring.
  • Using the same hash function f, we map servers based on server IP or name onto the ring.
  1. Server Lookup
  2. A key's server is determined by traversing clockwise on the ring until a server is found.
  1. Adding and Removing Servers
  2. Adding a server redistributes only nearby keys. Only a fraction of keys are redistributed to the new server.
  • Removing a server affects only the keys in its range. Only keys from the removed server are reassigned to the next server clockwise.

Interview questions and answers

Explain consistent hashing in simple words.
Put servers and keys on a circle using a hash. Each key belongs to the first server found going clockwise. When a server is added or removed, only the keys next to it move.
What happens to keys when a server is removed?
Only the keys that belonged to it are reassigned, to the next server clockwise. Other keys do not move.
What happens when a server is added?
Only the keys between the new server and its anticlockwise neighbour move to the new server.
Cross question: How do you find the next server quickly?
Keep the server positions in a sorted structure (sorted array or balanced tree) and use binary search to find the first position at or after the key's hash, wrapping around to the start if needed.
Cross question: Why use the same hash function for servers and keys?
So both live in the same hash space, which lets us compare their positions on the ring.

🎲 Virtual nodes: fixing uneven distribution

Hinglish samajh: Basic ring mein do samasyayein hain: kuch servers ko ring ka bahut bada hissa mil jaata hai aur kuch ko bahut chhota, aur keys bhi barabar nahi bantti. Iska hal hai virtual nodes: har real server ko ring par kai baar alag alag naam se rakhte hain (jaise s0#0, s0#1, s0#2). Isse har server ke paas kai chhote slices hote hain jo average ho jaate hain. Hamare simulation mein 1 point per server par keys 7529, 1510, 687 aur 274 mili, jabki 100 virtual nodes par lagbhag barabar (2554, 2562, 2775, 2109). Kharcha: ring ke liye zyada memory.

The basic ring has two problems. First, it is impossible to keep the partition sizes equal: some servers happen to land close together and get a small slice of the ring, while others get a very large slice. Second, the keys themselves may not be spread evenly, so some servers receive many more keys than others. A server with a huge slice becomes a hotspot.

The solution is virtual nodes (also called replicas). Instead of putting each real server on the ring once, we put it on the ring many times, under different virtual names (for example server0#0, server0#1, server0#2 and so on). Each virtual node is a separate point on the ring, and each belongs to the real server that created it. A key walks clockwise to the first virtual node and is stored on that node's real server.

With many small slices scattered around the ring, the unlucky big slice problem disappears, because each server owns many small slices that average out. As the number of virtual nodes grows, the distribution becomes more balanced (the standard deviation gets smaller). The cost is that we need more memory to store the virtual node positions. It is a trade-off: tune the number of virtual nodes to your needs. Virtual nodes also let you give stronger machines more virtual nodes, so they take a bigger share of the data.

The effect is easy to see in a simulation I ran with 10,000 keys on 4 servers using SHA-1. With one point per server, the servers received 7,529, 1,510, 687 and 274 keys, which is very uneven. With 100 virtual nodes per server, they received 2,554, 2,562, 2,775 and 2,109 keys, which is much closer to the ideal 2,500 each.

Simulation: 10,000 keys on 4 servers (SHA-1)

SetupServer AServer BServer CServer DVerdict
1 point per server7,5291,510687274Very uneven
100 virtual nodes per server2,5542,5622,7752,109Close to 2,500 each

✨ Features

  • Each real server appears many times on the ring.
  • Virtual nodes spread the load evenly.
  • More virtual nodes means a smaller standard deviation of load.

✅ Benefits

  • Much better balance of keys.
  • Heterogeneous servers can get different shares.
  • Failure of one server spreads its load over many others, not just one neighbour.

⚠️ Problems

  • More virtual nodes use more memory for the ring.
  • Lookups have more points to search.
  • Changes touch many ring positions.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Challenges and Solutions

Two Issues in Basic Approach

  1. Uneven Partition Sizes: Servers may have unequal data partitions.
  2. Non-uniform Key Distribution: Some servers may receive significantly more keys than others.

Solution: Virtual Nodes

  • Each server is represented by multiple virtual nodes on the ring uniformly distrubuted on the ring.
  • Virtual nodes improve key distribution and balance load. As the number of virtual nodes increases, the distribution of keys becomes more balanced. This is because the standard deviation gets smaller with more virtual nodes, leading to balanced data distribution.

Interview questions and answers

What are virtual nodes and why use them?
They are multiple points on the ring for each real server. They even out the data distribution because each server owns many small slices instead of one big or small slice.
What is the trade-off?
More virtual nodes give better balance but need more memory to store the ring, so choose a number that balances both.
Cross question: How do virtual nodes help with different server sizes?
Give a more powerful server more virtual nodes so it receives proportionally more keys.
Cross question: What happens when a server with virtual nodes fails?
Its many small slices are taken over by many different neighbours, so the extra load is spread out rather than falling on a single next server.

🎯 Which keys are affected when servers change?

Hinglish samajh: Server jodte ya hatate samay kaun si keys hilti hain? Naya server jodne par us server se ghadi ki ulti disha mein pichhle server tak ki keys (jaise s3 aur s4 ke beech) naye server par aati hain. Server hatane par us server aur uske pichhle server (jaise s0 aur s1) ke beech ki keys agle server (s2) par jaati hain. Baaki keys wahin rehti hain. Isiliye 4 se 5 servers par lagbhag 20% keys hilti hain, jabki modulo mein lagbhag 79%.

It helps to know exactly which keys move, because it tells you how much work a scaling event creates. The rule is the same in both directions: look at the ring and find the stretch of the ring between the changed server and its predecessor, the previous server going anticlockwise.

When a server is added. Suppose server 4 is added to a ring that has servers 0 to 3. Start at server 4 and move anticlockwise until you reach another server, which is server 3. The keys located between server 3 and server 4 used to belong to the next server clockwise, and they now need to be moved to server 4. All the other keys stay put.

When a server is removed. Suppose server 1 is removed. Start at server 1 and move anticlockwise until you reach another server, which is server 0. The keys between server 0 and server 1 used to be owned by server 1. They must be redistributed to the next server clockwise, which is server 2. Again, no other keys are affected.

This is why scaling is gentle with consistent hashing. If you have N servers and add one, on average only about 1/(N+1) of the keys move (about 20% when going from 4 to 5 servers; my simulation with 100 virtual nodes measured 19.3%). Compare that with about 79% for the modulo approach.

Fraction of keys that move when going from 4 to 5 servers

MethodKeys moved (10,000-key simulation)Ideal
hash % Nabout 79%much higher than needed
Consistent hashing with 100 virtual nodes per serverabout 19%about 20% (1 out of 5)

✨ Features

  • The affected range is the arc between a changed server and its predecessor.
  • Adding a server moves roughly 1/(N+1) of the keys.
  • Removing a server moves only that server's keys.

✅ Benefits

  • Predictable, small data movement.
  • Caches stay mostly warm during scaling.
  • Planned maintenance has limited impact.

⚠️ Problems

  • The new server starts empty and must receive data before it can serve well.
  • The affected servers handle extra transfer load during the move.
  • With uneven ring slices, one change may still move more than average.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Affected Keys

When servers are added or removed:

  • Added Server: Affected keys are those between the new server and its predecessor. In the following example server 4 is added onto the ring. The affected range starts from s4 (newly added node) and moves anticlockwise around the ring until a server is found (s3). Thus, keys located between s3 and s4 need to be redistributed to s4.
  • Removed Server: Affected keys are those between the removed server and its predecessor. In the following example when a server (s1) is removed, the affected range starts from s1 (removed node) and moves anticlockwise around the ring until a server is found (s0). Thus, keys located between s0 and s1 must be redistributed to s2.

Interview questions and answers

Which keys move when a server is added?
Those between the new server and its predecessor (going anticlockwise). They move to the new server.
Which keys move when a server is removed?
Only the keys that belonged to it. They go to the next server clockwise.
Cross question: Roughly what fraction moves when adding the 5th server?
About one fifth (1 out of 5) with a balanced ring, far less than the roughly 80% for modulo hashing.
Cross question: Do you have to move the data immediately?
For a cache, you can let misses fill the new server naturally. For a database, you must copy the affected range before switching traffic, and keep replicas to avoid data loss.

🏆 Benefits and real-world applications

Hinglish samajh: Consistent hashing ke fayde: keys ka kam se kam hilna, aasan horizontal scaling aur hotspots se bachav (virtual nodes ke saath). Ye Amazon DynamoDB, Apache Cassandra, Discord, Akamai CDN aur Maglev load balancer mein use hota hai. Interview mein jab bhi kaha jaye ki data ya requests aise servers par baanto jo badalte rehte hain, to consistent hashing, hash ring aur virtual nodes ka naam lo aur samjhao ki kitna kam data hilta hai.

Let us collect what consistent hashing gives you. The first benefit is minimized redistribution: only a fraction of keys is reassigned when servers come and go. The second is scalability: you can add servers to grow the system and remove servers to shrink it without a big migration. The third is that it mitigates hotspots: with virtual nodes the data is spread evenly, so no single server gets overloaded, and a failed server's load is shared by many others.

It is used in many production systems. Amazon DynamoDB and Apache Cassandra use it to partition data across nodes. Discord uses it to spread load across its servers. The Akamai CDN uses it to decide which edge server caches which content. Google's Maglev load balancer uses a form of consistent hashing so that a connection keeps going to the same backend even when the pool changes.

In an interview, if the problem is "distribute data or requests across servers that can change", say the words consistent hashing, draw the ring, mention virtual nodes, and explain how little data moves. Next chapter (the key-value store) uses it for partitioning, so this knowledge is directly reused.

Where consistent hashing is used

SystemTypical use
Amazon DynamoDBPartitioning data across storage nodes
Apache CassandraPartitioning and replica placement on a ring
DiscordSpreading load across servers
Akamai CDNDeciding which edge server holds which content
Maglev load balancerKeeping connections on the same backend as the pool changes

✨ Features

  • Minimized redistribution of keys.
  • Easy horizontal scaling.
  • Balanced load through virtual nodes.

✅ Benefits

  • Smooth scaling and failure handling.
  • Better cache hit rates during changes.
  • Proven in large production systems.

⚠️ Problems

  • Needs careful implementation of the ring and virtual nodes.
  • Does not by itself provide replication or consistency.
  • Hotspots can still happen for very popular keys.

Interview questions and answers

List the benefits of consistent hashing.
Minimized key redistribution, easy horizontal scaling, and mitigation of hotspots through even distribution.
Name systems that use it.
Amazon DynamoDB, Apache Cassandra, Discord, Akamai CDN and the Maglev load balancer.
Cross question: Does consistent hashing handle a very popular key?
No. If one key is extremely hot, its server is overloaded whatever the ring looks like. You need caching, replication of that key, or splitting it into several keys.
Cross question: Is it only for caches?
No. It also partitions databases, balances load between servers and places content in CDNs.

💻 Hands-on: a hash ring in code

Hinglish samajh: Code mein ring ek sorted list hai jisme har position ek real server ki taraf point karti hai. Har server ko kai virtual nodes ke saath jodte hain. Lookup ke liye key ka hash nikalte hain aur binary search se pehli position dhundte hain jo us hash ke baraabar ya badi ho; agar list ke aakhir se aage nikal jayein to shuruaat par wapas aa jaate hain (poora gola). Server jodna ya hatana sirf usi ke virtual nodes ko chhoota hai, isliye zyadatar keys wahin rehti hain. Ye code meri taraf se ek udaharan hai.

To make the idea concrete, here is a small hash ring written in C#. (This code is my own illustration, not from the repository.) It follows exactly the steps of the earlier lessons. The ring is a sorted list of positions, each pointing to a real server. Every server is added several times as virtual nodes. To look up a key, we hash it and use binary search to find the first position greater than or equal to the key's hash. If we go past the end of the list, we wrap around to the first position, which is exactly walking clockwise around a circle.

Adding or removing a server only inserts or deletes that server's virtual nodes. No other server's positions change, which is why most keys stay where they are. In production systems this code is wrapped with extras: replication to the next few servers on the ring, health checks, and a safe way to move data to the new owner before switching.

Try it with a few thousand keys and count how many keys change owner when you add a server. You should see roughly 1 / (N+1) of them move, which is the whole point.

Reading the code against the theory

ConceptWhere it appears in the code
Hash ringThe sorted dictionary of positions and the sorted key array
Virtual nodesThe loop that adds server + "#" + i
Clockwise lookupBinary search for the first position at or after the key hash
Wrap aroundIf the index passes the last element, use index 0
Add or remove serverInsert or delete only that server's virtual nodes

A minimal consistent hash ring (C#)

using System.Security.Cryptography;
using System.Text;

public class HashRing
{
    private readonly SortedDictionary<uint, string> ring = new();
    private uint[] keys = Array.Empty<uint>();
    private readonly int virtualNodes;

    public HashRing(int virtualNodes = class="nu">100) { this.virtualNodes = virtualNodes; }

    static uint Hash(string s)
    {
        var bytes = SHA1.HashData(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(s));
        return BitConverter.ToUInt32(bytes, class="nu">0);        ␀class="nu">0␀
    }

    public void AddServer(string server)
    {
        for (int i = class="nu">0; i < virtualNodes; i++)
            ring[Hash(server + "␀class="nu">1␀
        keys = ring.Keys.ToArray();                    ␀class="nu">2␀
    }

    public void RemoveServer(string server)
    {
        for (int i = class="nu">0; i < virtualNodes; i++)
            ring.Remove(Hash(server + "␀class="nu">3␀
        keys = ring.Keys.ToArray();
    }

    public string GetServer(string key)
    {
        uint h = Hash(key);
        int idx = Array.BinarySearch(keys, h);
        if (idx < class="nu">0) idx = ~idx;                       ␀class="nu">4␀
        if (idx == keys.Length) idx = class="nu">0;               ␀class="nu">5␀
        return ring[keys[idx]];
    }
}

✨ Features

  • Sorted ring plus binary search for lookup.
  • Virtual nodes for balance.
  • Add and remove only touch that server's points.

✅ Benefits

  • Short, readable implementation of the idea.
  • Lookup is O(log n) in the number of ring points.
  • Easy to test by counting moved keys.

⚠️ Problems

  • The array is rebuilt on every change in this simple version.
  • No replication, health checks or data migration.
  • A single process; a real system must share the ring layout across all clients.

Interview questions and answers

How do you implement the lookup efficiently?
Store the ring positions in a sorted array or tree and use binary search to find the first position at or after the key's hash, wrapping around to the start if needed.
Cross question: What is the time complexity of a lookup?
O(log M) where M is the number of virtual nodes, because of the binary search.
Cross question: How do clients agree on the ring?
They use the same hash function and the same list of servers and virtual node count, shared through configuration or a coordination service.
How would you test your implementation?
Add a server and count how many keys change owner. It should be close to 1/(N+1). Also check that servers receive similar numbers of keys.
